chapters.title: Chapter 5: Integrity Signals in Filings and Behaviour

lessons.title: Accounting Choices as a Character Test

body.text: Two companies with identical businesses can legally report very different profits. The gap is made of choices, and the same management makes those choices every single year.

children.text: Indian Accounting Standards do not produce one correct profit number. They leave management room to decide when revenue is recognised, what is capitalised rather than expensed, how long assets last, and when a doubtful receivable becomes a provision. Every one of those decisions is legal, disclosed, and signed off by the auditor. Taken together, over several years, they tell you whether management wants the reported numbers to flatter it or to be right. That is why accounting policy is a governance topic and not just an accounting one.

body.text: This lesson is not about detecting fraud. It is about detecting appetite. A management team that consistently picks the profit-flattering option in every grey area is telling you what it will do when a grey area becomes a black one.

body.caption: Where management has room to choose

cells: Revenue timing
Recognise on delivery, possession, or completion
Recognise early on percentage of completion, or push stock to distributors near year end
Significant accounting policies note; receivable and inventory days
Development and project costs
Expense R&D and project spending as incurred
Capitalise development costs and interest during construction
Intangible assets note; capital work in progress; finance cost note
Depreciation
Shorter useful lives, in line with Schedule II
Longer useful lives, or extending lives mid-way
Property, plant and equipment note; changes in estimates note
Provisioning
Provide early for doubtful receivables, slow inventory, and disputed dues
Delay provisions and call them one-time when they finally arrive
Expected credit loss note; exceptional items
Goodwill and investments
Test and impair promptly when a business underperforms
Defer impairment for years on optimistic projections
Goodwill and impairment notes; Key Audit Matters
Contingent liabilities
Provide when a claim becomes likely
Keep large tax or regulatory claims in the contingent note indefinitely
Contingent liabilities note

children.text: How Much Difference Can a Choice Make?

Take a company with a gross block of ₹12,000 crore, depreciated on a straight line basis. Management reviews useful lives and extends them from 10 years to 15 years. Nothing physical changes. No cash moves. The machines do not become better.

stats.label: Profit before tax effect
stats.context: About ₹300 crore of extra reported profit after tax at 25%

children.text: A change in useful life is a change in accounting estimate, so it is applied from the current year onwards and disclosed in the notes. It is entirely legal. But a company that extends asset lives in a weak year has borrowed profit from future years, and operating cash flow will not move at all. That divergence is the clue.

body.title: Capitalise or Expense?
body.prompt: A company spends ₹300 crore on product development during the year. Instead of expensing it, it capitalises the full amount as an intangible asset and amortises it over five years, starting the same year. Ignoring tax, by how much is profit before tax higher this year than if the whole amount had been expensed?
body.explanation: Expensing hits profit by ₹300 crore. Capitalising hits profit only by the first year of amortisation, ₹300 crore ÷ 5 = ₹60 crore. The difference is ₹240 crore of extra reported profit before tax, with no difference in cash spent. The cash flow statement shows it: the ₹300 crore moves from operating outflow to investing outflow, which also flatters operating cash flow.

body.text: Capitalisation has a second effect that is easy to miss. Money spent on development or interest during construction leaves operating cash flow and appears under investing activities instead. So aggressive capitalisation improves reported profit and reported operating cash flow at the same time, which is why free cash flow, after capex, is the harder number to dress up.

children.text: The Master Test: Does Profit Turn Into Cash?

You cannot audit a company from your desk, and you do not need to. Almost every aggressive accounting choice produces the same symptom: profit rises faster than cash. Track the ratio of operating cash flow to EBITDA over five years, and cumulative operating cash flow against cumulative net profit. Honest, cash-generative businesses keep those ratios high and stable. Companies leaning on accounting choices show a steady decline.

body.latex: \text{Cash Conversion} = \frac{\text{Cash Flow from Operations}}{\text{EBITDA}} \qquad \text{5-Year Check} = \frac{\sum \text{CFO}}{\sum \text{Net Profit}}
body.caption: Use five years to smooth out working capital swings in any single year

body.title: Cash flow from operations as a share of EBITDA

children.text: Company B's profits look fine every year. Its cash conversion has more than halved in five years. Somewhere in that gap sit rising receivables, growing inventory, capitalised costs, or revenue booked before anyone paid. You do not need to know which one it is to know that the earnings are getting worse in quality even as they improve on paper.
Working Capital Days: The Second Reading

Screener.in shows debtor days, inventory days, and cash conversion cycle for ten years on every company page. If revenue grows 15% while receivables grow 55%, the extra sales were made on credit that the company may not collect. A company with revenue of ₹4,000 crore and receivables of ₹700 crore is collecting in about 64 days. If revenue rises to ₹4,600 crore and receivables jump to ₹1,100 crore, collection has stretched to about 87 days, and roughly ₹400 crore of reported growth is sitting in someone else's hands.

body.title: The Quality Check
body.textWithBlank: The simplest single test of earnings quality is to compare cumulative cash flow from operations with cumulative ___ over five years.
body.explanation: Over one year, working capital swings and timing can distort the comparison. Over five years, a company whose cumulative operating cash flow is far below cumulative profit is reporting earnings that never turned into money.

children.text: Revenue timing is not a small detail. When Ind AS 115 came into force for Indian companies from April 2018, real estate developers had to move from recognising revenue as construction progressed to recognising it largely on handover of possession. Reported revenue and profit at many developers fell sharply, even though the underlying construction and sales activity was unchanged. The same projects, the same cash, a different rule for when profit appears.

Contingent liabilities are not theoretical either. After the Supreme Court's October 2019 ruling on adjusted gross revenue dues, Indian telecom companies had to provide for amounts that had sat in contingent liability notes for years. Bharti Airtel reported a quarterly loss of about ₹23,045 crore in the September 2019 quarter, then among the largest ever reported by an Indian company, and Vodafone Idea's loss was larger still. Anyone who had read the contingent liabilities note knew the size of the claim long before it hit the profit and loss account.

And provisioning is where accounting choice shades into something worse. Yes Bank, from Lesson 1, was not accused of inventing revenue. Its problem was recognising bad loans late, which RBI's inspections repeatedly flagged as divergence. Late provisioning is the most common bridge between an aggressive choice and a misstatement.

columns.label: Conservative Signals
points: Cash conversion consistently high and stable
R&D and development costs expensed as incurred
Useful lives in line with Schedule II and unchanged for years
Provisions taken early, with the reasons explained
Few or no exceptional items, and stable accounting policies

columns.label: Aggressive Signals
points: Profit growing while cash conversion falls year after year
Large capital work in progress or intangibles under development that never start depreciating
Useful lives extended, or estimates changed, in a weak year
Exceptional items in most years, always presented as one-offs
Other income, forex gains, or asset sales carrying a large share of profit

body.title: Which Choice Is Most Aggressive?
body.question: Four companies each made one accounting decision this year. Which is the most aggressive?
options: A pharma company expensed its entire ₹450 crore R&D spend, as it has done for a decade
A cement company recognised an impairment on an underperforming plant after two years of losses there
An engineering company extended the useful life of its plant and machinery from 12 to 18 years in a year when order inflows fell, adding ₹260 crore to profit before tax
A consumer company disclosed a ₹90 crore tax dispute in contingent liabilities and explained why it expects to win
body.explanation: Extending useful lives in a weak year converts an operational shortfall into a reported profit without any change in the business or in cash. The other three are conservative or routine: expensing R&D, impairing promptly, and disclosing a dispute clearly all reduce or reveal risk rather than hide it.

body.title: The Company Whose Profit Never Arrives
body.scenario: A mid cap industrial automation company on NSE has grown reported profit at 22% a year for five years. Reading the annual reports you find: cumulative operating cash flow over those five years is ₹1,100 crore against cumulative net profit of ₹2,600 crore; debtor days have risen from 68 to 119; capital work in progress has grown from ₹210 crore to ₹1,450 crore, with one project shown as under construction for four years; interest during construction is being capitalised; development costs of ₹180 crore a year are capitalised as intangibles; and there has been an exceptional item in four of the five years. The auditor's opinion is unmodified, with a Key Audit Matter on revenue recognition.
body.prompt: What is your assessment, and what would you check next?
body.modelAnswer: The reported profit is real on paper and largely absent in cash: five years of profit converted into less than half as much operating cash flow. Each finding explains part of the gap. Debtor days rising from 68 to 119 means a large share of the growth is unpaid sales. Capital work in progress growing seven times with a project under construction for four years means costs, including capitalised interest, are parked on the balance sheet instead of running through the P&L, and an asset that never gets commissioned never starts depreciating. Capitalised development costs add another ₹180 crore a year of expenses deferred. Exceptional items in four of five years are not exceptional, they are recurring costs excluded from the headline. The clean audit opinion does not contradict any of this, because all of these choices can be legal, which is exactly the point, and the Key Audit Matter on revenue recognition shows the auditor focused there too. Next, check whether the long-running project has a commissioning date and any capitalised interest disclosure, recompute profit expensing development costs and adding back exceptional items, ask on the concall when the project starts depreciating, and check whether receivables are concentrated in a few customers or any related parties. Until cash conversion improves, treat the growth as unproven and value the company on cash, not earnings.

body.title: Run an Earnings Quality Check
steps: On screener.in, compare cumulative cash flow from operations with cumulative net profit for the last five and ten years
Plot CFO divided by EBITDA for five years and look for a downward trend
Check debtor days, inventory days, and the cash conversion cycle over ten years against revenue growth
In the annual report, read the significant accounting policies note and compare it with the previous year, looking for any change in revenue recognition, useful lives, or provisioning
Check capital work in progress and intangibles under development: how long have they been there, and is interest being capitalised?
Add up exceptional items over five years and recompute profit including them
Read the contingent liabilities note and size the largest claims against net worth
Compare the auditor's Key Audit Matters with the areas you have flagged

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are discussed based on published financial statements, regulatory developments, and widely reported events, for education only. The numerical examples are illustrative. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security, or accounting advice.

points: Ind AS leaves genuine room for judgement, so identical businesses can report different profits legally; the pattern of choices reveals management's character
Extending useful lives from 10 to 15 years on a ₹12,000 crore gross block adds ₹400 crore to pre-tax profit while nothing changes in the business
Capitalising ₹300 crore of development cost instead of expensing it raises pre-tax profit by ₹240 crore in year one and flatters operating cash flow too
The master test is cash: track CFO divided by EBITDA for five years, and cumulative CFO against cumulative profit
Rising debtor and inventory days, long-lived capital work in progress, and recurring exceptional items are the usual sources of a profit to cash gap
Ind AS 115 in real estate, the telecom AGR provisions, and Yes Bank's NPA divergence show how timing and provisioning decisions eventually become real losses
